title: Using lifting to control your anxiety
summary: NH explains how lifting helps manage anxiety by acting as moving meditation and spending excess physical energy, but warns it can become a dependency. He recommends spreading training over more days, stopping when mental stamina runs out, and fixing a set program and diet instead of constantly changing them.
claims: Anxiety is the most widespread mental disorder; everyone has it at varying levels
Anxiety is energy; if it isn't spent it will destroy you
His anxiety comes from not being productive, and obsessing over small details spirals it
Once technique and program are ingrained, lifting becomes mindfulness: your body is busy so your mind can rest
People who struggle with meditation will find meditating while lifting much more doable
Modern desk jobs exhaust the mind but leave the body full of energy, which creates anxiety; training fixes this
Post-workout endorphin highs usually kick in about three to four months after starting, then you get hooked
Relying on training to soothe anxiety means days you can't train become high-anxiety days
If anxiety worsens on three sessions a week, spread the same volume over four or five shorter sessions
Mental stamina is usually lower than physical stamina; stop the workout when your mind checks out and train again the next day
Grinding on after mental fatigue is like failing lifts constantly: you stop progressing
He trains six days a week for two to three hours and his one rest day tends to be high-anxiety
On rest days, manage anxiety with walks and time outside rather than relying only on training
Anxious lifters need an exact A-B-C-D plan; improvising feeds the anxiety
Set your diet (foods, calories, macros) and program, then don't touch them; constant tweaking makes you doubt and fuels anxiety
Change is the enemy of anxiety control; resist the urge to tweak
Try to master mild anxiety without medication; severe cases may need a chemical crutch
